title: India: Varna, Jati and Change
bigQuestion: How did a system of birth groups shape life in India, and how have people worked to change it?

story.title: The Boy on the Sack
story.kicker: A schoolboy was made to sit apart from his classmates, and he grew up to help write the rules for a whole nation.
paragraphs: In the 1890s a small boy named Bhimrao walked to school in the town of Satara, in western India. He carried a folded piece of sacking under his arm. His family belonged to the Mahar community. Many people at the time treated Mahars as untouchable, which meant others would not share food, water or even a floor mat with them.

At school Bhimrao spread his sack in a corner and sat on it, away from the other children. Some teachers would not touch his notebooks. When he was thirsty, he could not turn on the water tap himself. He had to wait for a school worker to pour water into his cupped hands from above. If no worker came, he went without.

Bhimrao was a hungry reader, and his father pushed him to study. He finished high school at a time when very few Mahar children did. Then he won scholarships to study abroad. He earned advanced degrees from Columbia University in New York and from the London School of Economics. People came to know him as Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.

Ambedkar spent his life fighting the rules that had shut him out. When India became independent in 1947, he was asked to chair the committee that drafted its new Constitution. That Constitution, in force from 1950, says that untouchability is abolished. The boy who once sat on a sack helped write the highest law of a nation of hundreds of millions.
story.think: What do you think it felt like for Ambedkar to write a law against the treatment he lived through as a child? Why might his own experience have mattered?

lessons.title: Four Groups in Old Texts
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Hindu texts described society as four broad groups called varnas.
reading: More than 3,000 years ago, poets in northern India composed hymns in the Sanskrit language. These hymns were collected in the Rig Veda, one of the oldest religious texts in the world. One hymn pictures society as the body of a great cosmic being. Different groups of people come from different parts of that body.

Later texts built on this picture. They named four *varnas*, or broad groups. Brahmins were priests and teachers. Kshatriyas were rulers and warriors. Vaishyas were traders and farmers. Shudras were laborers who served the other three. Each group was given its own duties, called *dharma*.

It helps to remember that varna was mostly an ideal written down by priests and scholars. It was a way of saying how society should be ordered. Real life was far messier. Kings sometimes came from families outside the warrior varna, and many people did work that did not match the old list.

words.d: one of four broad social groups described in ancient Hindu texts
in Hindu thought, a person's duty or right way of living
a collection of very old Sanskrit hymns, among the oldest religious texts in the world

look.title: A Society Pictured as a Body
look.text: Imagine a drawing of a giant human body. Priests come from the mouth. Warriors come from the arms. Traders and farmers come from the thighs. Laborers come from the feet. The drawing says every part is needed for the body to live. It also places the parts from top to bottom.
look.prompt: What two messages could a reader take from this picture? One is about working together. What is the other one about?

check.q: How many varnas did the ancient texts describe?
check.why: The texts named four varnas: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

check.q: Which varna was linked with priests and teachers?
check.why: Brahmins were the priests and teachers in the varna picture.

check.q: Why does the lesson call varna mostly an ideal?
choices: It was invented by British rulers
It described how society should be, and real life was messier
check.why: Varna was a plan written by priests and scholars; real jobs and rulers often did not match it.

lessons.title: Jati: Thousands of Birth Groups
lessons.mainIdea: In daily life, people belonged to a jati, a local birth group tied to work and marriage.
reading: Picture a village in India 200 years ago. One family makes clay pots. Another weaves cloth. Another washes clothes, and another works leather. Each family belongs to a group that has done this work for generations. Children are born into the group, and they usually marry inside it.

These birth groups are called *jatis*. The word comes from a root meaning birth. India had thousands of jatis, and they differed from region to region. A jati was often linked to a job, and it set rules about marriage, food and who could eat with whom. Some people ranked jatis as higher or lower in *purity*.

The Portuguese, who came to India around 1500, used their word casta, meaning breed or lineage. That word became caste in English. So when people say caste, they often mean jati. Varna was the broad four-part idea in the texts. Jati was the group a person actually lived in every day.

words.d: a local birth group, often tied to a kind of work and to marriage inside the group
an English word, from Portuguese casta, for birth groups such as jatis
an idea that some groups or acts are cleaner in a religious sense than others

look.title: Varna and Jati Side by Side
look.text: Varna: four groups, named in old religious texts, the same list all over India. Jati: thousands of groups, found in real villages and towns, different in each region, tied to a family's work and to who you may marry.
look.prompt: If you visited one village, which would you see more clearly, varna or jati? Explain why.

check.q: What does the word jati come from?
check.why: Jati comes from a root meaning birth, because people were born into their jati.

check.q: Where did the English word caste come from?
check.why: The Portuguese used casta, meaning breed or lineage, and it became caste in English.

check.q: How was jati different from varna?
choices: Jati was a local birth group people lived in every day
Jati appeared only in the Rig Veda
check.why: Varna was a broad four-part idea in texts; jatis were thousands of real local groups.

lessons.title: Outside the Four Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Some communities were pushed below the four varnas and treated as untouchable.
reading: Some jobs were seen as polluting. These included sweeping streets, removing dead animals, tanning leather and handling the dead at cremation grounds. The communities who did this work were often placed outside the four varnas altogether. Other people treated them as *untouchable*.

Being treated as untouchable meant daily rules of separation. In many places these communities could not draw water from the village well. They could not enter many temples. Some had to live at the edge of the village. These rules were enforced by custom and by pressure from powerful groups, and they varied by region.

Today many people from these communities call themselves *Dalit*. The word means broken or crushed in Marathi and Sanskrit. Leaders chose it with pride, to name the harm done to them and their shared strength. The Indian government uses the term Scheduled Castes for these communities in its laws.

words.d: an old label for groups whom others refused to touch or share with; now rejected and outlawed
a name many people once called untouchable chose for themselves; it means broken or crushed
the legal term the Indian government uses for Dalit communities

look.title: A Well in the Village
look.text: A village has one deep well with clean, cool water. For generations, one community has been told it may not use it. Its families walk a long way to a muddy stream instead. No written law says this. Everyone simply knows the rule, and breaking it brings punishment from neighbors.
look.prompt: How can a rule be powerful even if it is never written down? What would it take to change it?

check.q: Which kind of work was often seen as polluting?
check.why: Work such as tanning leather and removing dead animals was often labeled polluting.

check.q: What does the word Dalit mean?
check.why: Dalit means broken or crushed; leaders chose it to name the harm and their shared strength.

check.q: What term does the Indian government use in law for Dalit communities?
check.why: Indian laws use Scheduled Castes for these communities.

lessons.title: Voices Inside Hinduism
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindu poets, saints and reformers taught that devotion to God matters more than birth.
reading: In the 1400s a poet named Ravidas lived in the city of Varanasi. He came from a leather-working community that others looked down on. Yet he sang songs of love for God that people still sing today. His message was simple: God is found by a loving heart, not by a high birth.

Ravidas was part of the *bhakti* movement. Bhakti means loving devotion. Across many centuries, bhakti saints wrote in everyday languages instead of Sanskrit. Many of them, including women and people from low-ranked jatis, taught that anyone could reach God. Their songs spread through villages and gave people dignity.

Hindu reformers kept this work going in modern times. In the 1800s and 1900s, groups such as the Arya Samaj argued against untouchability. Mohandas Gandhi called it a sin and campaigned to open temples to all. Hinduism is a very large and varied faith, and its followers have long debated caste among themselves.

words.d: loving devotion to God; a movement of saints and poets who taught that anyone could reach God
a person who works to change and improve a system from the inside

look.title: A Song About the Heart
look.text: The poet says that God does not ask what family you were born into. God looks at the love in your heart. A leather worker who loves God is closer to God than a proud person of high birth.
look.cite: Ravidas, devotional songs, c. 1400s (summary of a common theme)
look.prompt: How does this song challenge the idea that birth decides a person's worth?

check.q: What does bhakti mean?
check.why: Bhakti means loving devotion to God.

check.q: What community did Ravidas come from?
check.why: Ravidas came from a leather-working community that others looked down on.

check.q: Which statement best fits the lesson?
choices: All Hindus have always agreed about caste
Hindus have long debated caste, and many worked against untouchability
check.why: The lesson shows bhakti saints and modern reformers inside Hinduism challenging caste.

lessons.title: Sikh, Muslim and Christian Responses
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhism, Islam and Christianity taught equality before God, though caste habits often lingered.
reading: In the 1500s Guru Nanak founded the Sikh faith in the Punjab region. He taught that all people are equal before one God. Sikhs set up the *langar*, a free community kitchen. Everyone sits on the floor together in rows and eats the same food, whatever their birth. Sikh temples still serve langar today.

Islam came to India through traders and rulers over many centuries. Islam teaches that all believers are equal before God, and people pray side by side in the mosque. Christianity also teaches equality before God. Over time, many people from low-ranked jatis became Muslims or Christians, partly hoping for more respect.

Yet customs are hard to change. Historians find that caste-like divisions often survived inside these communities too. Some families still married only within their old group. Some churches once had separate seating. So the teachings of these faiths opened a path, and their members have kept working to live up to them.

words.d: the free community kitchen at a Sikh temple, where everyone eats together
the idea that people have the same worth and deserve the same treatment

look.title: Sitting in Rows
look.text: Hundreds of people sit on long mats at a Sikh temple. A farmer sits next to a doctor. A child sits next to a stranger. Volunteers walk down the rows with pots of lentils and stacks of flatbread. Everyone gets the same food, served the same way.
look.prompt: What lesson about equality does the langar teach without using any words?

check.q: Who founded the Sikh faith?
check.why: Guru Nanak founded the Sikh faith in the Punjab in the 1500s.

check.q: What happens at a langar?
choices: Everyone eats together, whatever their birth
check.why: At the langar everyone sits together and eats the same free food.

check.q: What do historians find about caste in Muslim and Christian communities in India?
check.why: Customs are hard to change, so caste-like divisions often lingered inside these communities.

lessons.title: The Buddha and Later Buddhists
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha taught that actions, not birth, make a person worthy, and Ambedkar later turned to Buddhism.
reading: About 2,500 years ago, Siddhartha Gautama lived in northern India. He became known as the Buddha, which means awakened one. He welcomed people of every varna into his community of monks and nuns. He taught that a person becomes noble by good actions, not by birth.

Buddhism spread across Asia but became small in India itself over the centuries. Then, in 1956, B. R. Ambedkar held a large public ceremony in the city of Nagpur. He and a very large crowd of his followers, many of them Dalits, became Buddhists together. Ambedkar said he wanted a faith built on equality and reason.

Ambedkar's step is sometimes called a *conversion*, a change from one religion to another. It was also a political act. It showed that Dalits could choose their own path. Many Indian Buddhists today trace their faith to that day in Nagpur, just weeks before Ambedkar died.

words.d: a title meaning awakened one, given to Siddhartha Gautama, who founded Buddhism
a change from one religion to another

look.title: Noble by Actions
look.text: A person is not a Brahmin by birth, nor an outcast by birth. By actions one becomes an outcast, and by actions one becomes a Brahmin.
look.cite: Sutta Nipata, early Buddhist verses (common English rendering, Vasala Sutta)
look.prompt: What does the Buddha say decides a person's worth? How is that different from the jati system?

check.q: What does the title Buddha mean?
check.why: Buddha means awakened one.

check.q: What did Ambedkar do in Nagpur in 1956?
choices: He and many followers became Buddhists
check.why: In 1956 Ambedkar and a large crowd of followers became Buddhists in Nagpur.

check.q: According to the Buddha, what makes a person noble?
check.why: The Buddha taught that a person becomes noble by actions, not by birth.

lessons.title: Ambedkar's Struggle
lessons.mainIdea: Ambedkar led Dalits in peaceful protests to claim rights such as water and temple entry.
reading: In 1927, in the town of Mahad, there was a public water tank. By law it was open to all. By custom, Dalits were kept away. Ambedkar led thousands of people to the tank, and they drank from it together. This protest is called the Mahad *Satyagraha*, a word meaning holding firmly to truth.

Some upper-caste residents answered with violence, and the struggle went to court. Ambedkar kept organizing. He started newspapers, founded schools and hostels, and formed political groups. He told his followers to get an education, to organize and to demand their rights.

Ambedkar and Gandhi both opposed untouchability, but they disagreed on how to end it. In 1932 they argued over separate elections for Dalits. Gandhi feared this would split Hindus. They reached a deal called the *Poona Pact*, which reserved seats for Dalits instead. Historians still debate which approach did more good.

words.d: Gandhi's word for nonviolent protest; it means holding firmly to truth
a 1932 agreement between Ambedkar and Gandhi that reserved seats in elections for Dalits
a public action that shows people want something changed

look.title: Three Steps
look.text: Ambedkar urged his followers to get educated, to stir people to act, and to organize together so their voices would be heard.
look.cite: B. R. Ambedkar, speeches, 1940s (widely quoted as 'Educate, agitate, organize')
look.prompt: Why might Ambedkar have put education first in his list?

check.q: What happened at the Mahad tank in 1927?
choices: Dalits drank from a public tank they had been kept from
check.why: Ambedkar led thousands of Dalits to drink from the public tank at Mahad.

check.q: What was the Poona Pact?
choices: A 1932 deal that reserved election seats for Dalits
check.why: The Poona Pact of 1932 reserved seats for Dalits instead of separate elections.

check.q: How did Ambedkar and Gandhi relate on untouchability?
choices: Both opposed it but disagreed on how to end it
check.why: Both opposed untouchability, but they disagreed about methods such as separate elections.

lessons.title: Writing the Constitution
lessons.mainIdea: India's Constitution of 1950, drafted under Ambedkar's lead, abolished untouchability.
reading: India won independence from Britain in 1947. The new country needed a *constitution*, a set of highest laws that says how the government works and what rights people have. An assembly of elected members debated it for almost three years. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which wrote and revised the text.

The Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950. Indians celebrate that day as Republic Day. It promises every citizen equality before the law. It forbids unfair treatment because of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 17 says that untouchability is abolished and that practicing it in any form is forbidden.

To *abolish* something is to end it by law. Ambedkar knew a law alone could not change every heart overnight. Still, it changed the rules. Now a Dalit who was turned away from a well or a shop could go to the police and the courts. The state was on the side of equality.

words.d: a country's highest set of laws, describing the government and people's rights
to end something officially by law
January 26, the day India celebrates its Constitution coming into force in 1950

look.title: Article 17
look.text: Untouchability is abolished, and practicing it in any form is forbidden. Enforcing any disadvantage that comes from untouchability is a crime punishable by law.
look.prompt: This article has two parts. What does the first part do? What does the second part add?

check.q: What role did Ambedkar play in writing India's Constitution?
choices: He wrote only the preamble's title
check.why: Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee that wrote and revised the text.

check.q: When did India's Constitution come into force?
check.why: It came into force on January 26, 1950, now celebrated as Republic Day.

check.q: What does Article 17 do?
check.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes practicing it a crime.

lessons.title: Reservations in Schools and Jobs
lessons.mainIdea: India reserves a share of college seats, government jobs and elected seats for groups held back by caste.
reading: Imagine two students who both want to become engineers. One comes from a family of teachers with books at home. The other is the first in her family to finish school, from a community long kept out of classrooms. India's Constitution asked: how do we give the second student a fair chance?

One answer is *reservations*. A share of seats in public colleges, government jobs and elected bodies is set aside for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Scheduled Tribes are Indigenous communities, often called Adivasis. In the 1990s reservations were also extended to many groups called Other Backward Classes.

Supporters say reservations have helped millions of families enter colleges, offices and parliament for the first time. Critics say seats should go by merit or by family income, not by group, and that the better-off in each group gain most. Courts have set limits, and the debate continues.

words.d: in India, a share of seats in schools, jobs and legislatures set aside for groups held back by caste
the legal term in India for Indigenous communities, also called Adivasis
choosing people by their skills and test results

look.title: Who Counts in the Census
look.prompt: About what share of India's people belonged to Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes combined in 2011?

check.q: What are reservations in India?
choices: Seats set aside for groups held back by caste
check.why: Reservations set aside seats in colleges, jobs and legislatures for groups held back by caste.

check.q: Who are Scheduled Tribes?
check.why: Scheduled Tribes are Indigenous communities, often called Adivasis.

check.q: What is one criticism of reservations named in the lesson?
choices: They are too new to judge
Seats should go by merit or income, not group
check.why: Critics argue for merit or family income, and say the better-off in each group gain most.

lessons.title: Change, Hope and Unfinished Work
lessons.mainIdea: Caste has weakened in many areas of life, but it still shapes marriage, work and politics for many.
reading: In 1997 K. R. Narayanan became President of India. He was born into a Dalit family in Kerala, in a thatched hut. He was the first Dalit to hold the country's highest office. His life shows how much can change within one lifetime.

In big cities, people of different jatis ride the same trains, study together and work side by side. Many young people choose their own partners. Yet surveys find most marriages in India still happen inside the same caste. Laws such as a 1989 act punish attacks on Dalits and Adivasis, because such attacks still happen.

Indians disagree about the way forward. Some want caste counted in every census so help can be aimed well. Others fear counting keeps caste alive. Some say rising incomes will end it; others say only laws and movements will. Caste is a question inside India, never a verdict on Hindus or any faith.

words.d: treating people unfairly because of the group they belong to
an official count of a country's people

look.title: Religions in India
look.prompt: Caste-like divisions appear in more than one of these faiths. Why does that suggest caste is about social custom as well as religion?

check.q: What is one debate the lesson describes?

check.why: Some want caste counted so help can be aimed well; others fear counting keeps caste alive.
